Gender: Female	 
DOB: [redacted]

Hospital Course: 

The patient was admitted due to chronic anicteric cholestasis and worsening cough with exertional dyspnea. She was diagnosed with chronic Budd-Chiari syndrome (BCS) complicating sarcoidosis, which was confirmed by histopathological examination of the liver, gastric, and skin biopsies. The patient received treatment with oral prednisolone and warfarin anticoagulation therapy, and was discharged in stable condition.

Summary of Findings:

- Diabetes mellitus evolving for 3 years, without a history of oral contraceptive therapy.
- Increased cholestatic enzymes, including a γ-glutamyl transferase level of 136 UI/L and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) of 325 UI/L.
- Normocytic inflammatory anemia with hemoglobin of 10.6 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume of 82.8 fL, and serum ferritin of 150 g/L.
- Hepatomegaly with hypertrophied caudate lobe, splenomegaly, and porto-systemic collateral circulation, as confirmed by abdominal ultrasound with Doppler and abdominal CT.
- Multinodular liver, absence of hepatic veins, centrolobular hepatocytes that were focally atrophic and replaced by fibrous and inflammatory septa, and fibrosis, as confirmed by abdominal CT and liver biopsy.
- Mediastinal and hilar adenopathies with multiple micronodular opacities on the lower pulmonary lobes, as confirmed by chest CT.
- Non-caseating granuloma on gastric biopsies and sarcoid granulomas on skin lesion biopsies, without damage to bile ducts, as confirmed by histopathological examination.
- Raised angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) of 201 UECA.
- Negative results for tuberculin testing and bronchoalveolar lavage.

Hospital Course:

The patient was started on oral prednisolone at a dose of 1 mg/kg and warfarin anticoagulation therapy. Additional examinations were performed to screen for an underlying thrombophilic disorder but failed to ascertain an underlying prothrombotic condition. The diagnosis of BCS complicating sarcoidosis was the most likely. The patient responded well to the treatment and was discharged in stable condition.

Discharge:

The patient was discharged in stable condition with instructions for continuing oral prednisolone and warfarin anticoagulation therapy. Follow-up appointments were scheduled with the primary care physician and specialist providers. The patient was advised to monitor symptoms and report any changes or concerns. The patient and their family were counseled on the importance of adherence to medications, lifestyle modifications, and attendance at scheduled appointments.

Discharge Summary

Patient: [Name], Female, 26 years old

Admission Date: [Date]
Discharge Date: [Date]

Chief Complaint: Profound hearing loss in the left ear, tinnitus, and dizziness

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our department in 2011 with a complaint of profound hearing loss in her left ear. She also reported experiencing tinnitus and dizziness. She did not have nystagmus during physical examination, and advanced vestibular tests were not conducted. Tonal audiometry revealed a 37-dB hearing loss in the left ear with 70% speech discrimination, while the right ear showed normal range pure tone audiometry.

Radiological examinations showed a left cerebellopontine angle (CPA) mass that encased the left VIII cranial nerve. A key finding was a 4 mm diameter lesion in the internal auditory canal (IAC), also with radiological features corresponding to a left CPA lipoma. The patient was followed up clinically and radiologically for two years, during which time there was no progression of the lipoma.

Diagnosis: Left cerebellopontine angle (CPA) lipoma

The patient was discharged in a stable condition.

Discharge Instructions and Follow-up:

The patient is advised to undergo routine follow-up with an otolaryngologist, as per their physician's instructions.

Follow-up Imaging: CT/MRI after the physician prescribes.

Signed,

[Physician], MD

Discharge Summary:

Patient Identification:
The patient is a 57-year-old male with a history of extensive tobacco use, nonischemic cardiomyopathy, and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status (PS) of 3.

Hospital Course:
The patient received mechanical cardiac support with an LVAD due to severe heart failure after successfully completing initial evaluation. Three months after the surgery, mediastinal widening was noted on a chest X-ray performed for dyspnea and cough. CT scans revealed mediastinal lymphadenopathy without evidence of disease outside the chest. Mediastinoscopy was performed and pathologic examination showed consistent SCLC. 

Treatment Strategy:
The patient was removed from active consideration for cardiac transplantation. Chemotherapy was administered while hospitalized for close monitoring. Carboplatin and IV etoposide were given. After his first cycle of chemotherapy, the patient elected not to receive further chemotherapy and workup.

Complications:
The treatment course was complicated by cellulitis, neutropenic fevers with pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, and protracted nausea and vomiting. The patient was treated with a prolonged IV antibiotic course. Although the renal function remained within normal limits, the patient developed signs of worsening overload with left-sided pleural effusion and peripheral edema. 

Outcome: 
The patient elected for hospice care and was discharged home. The patient passed away about 6 months after the administration of chemotherapy.

Patient was admitted to the hospital for carcinoma of the right breast with enlarged axillary lymph nodes. She was given neoadjuvant systemic therapy with the nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor anastrozole (Arimidex®) and the CDK 4/6 inhibitor abemaciclib (Verzenio®) as part of a clinical trial (NeoMONARCH). Following this, adjuvant radiotherapy (RTX) of the right breast and the supraclavicular region was done in three-dimensional (3D) conformal technique. During the course of radiation, the patient developed a moderate acute radiodermatitis with small circumscribed moist epitheliolysis in the submammary fold.

After completion of RTX, the patient developed a 2cm wide circumscribed cutis edema at the irradiated breast, which later grew to cover the whole former irradiation field, with a continuous inflammatory infiltrate, hyperpigmentation, induration, and a loss of breast volume. To rule out a recurrence of lymphangiosis carcinomatosa cutis, a targeted punch biopsy was performed. The histology showed no signs of malignant tumor cells but a pronounced dermal fibrosis with thickened dermis and fibrosis extending into the underlying fatty tissue, with corresponding panniculitis and pronounced chronic perivascular inflammation.

After re-examination, the patient was diagnosed with postradiogenic circumscribed scleroderma 20 months after RTX. The patient declined suggested treatments, which included systemic immune suppression with steroids and methotrexate (MTX) but sought relief through the use of topical steroids and lymph drainage at a specialized center. The clinical picture has remained unchanged since December 2017. 

Instructions were given for the patient to be followed closely with scheduled checkups and monitoring. The patient was discharged with follow-up care plan. Informed consent was provided for the follow-up treatment plan.

- The patient should regularly monitor the condition of the affected areas

Hospital Course: 
The patient presented with complaints of burning, itching, pain, stinging, lacrimation, and decreased vision in her left eye. She reported sand splash to her eyes at the seaside three months prior and had discontinued contact lens wear ten days before admission to the clinic. Biomicroscopic examination of the left eye revealed central keratitis and corneal scraping sample was taken and inoculated for testing. Acanthamoeba sp. cysts were identified in the direct Giemsa stained specimen of corneal scraping. 

Treatment: 
The patient was treated with alternating topical fortified vancomycin, ceftazidime, propamidine isothionate 0.1% and chlorhexidine at ophthalmology clinic. Contact lenses and contact lens solution could not be cultured since they had been disposed of by the patient.

Follow-up: 
At the 2nd month visit, no growth was identified after inoculation of corneal scraping specimen onto E. coli plated NNA agar. The corneal scraping specimen was defined as "T2" genotype "A. castellani" according to PCR and sequence analysis that targeted 18S rDNA region performed. 

Conclusion: 
The patient's case report was approved by the Ethics Committee at Uludag University Faculty of Medicine (2016-9/18), and informed consent was obtained from the patient.

Discharge Date: [redacted]

Discharge Diagnosis: Pituitary germinoma, central diabetes insipidus
Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital due to an eight-month history of generalized fatigue, increased thirst, increased urinary frequency and volume, reduced nocturnal erections, decreased sexual desire, weight loss of 18 kg in six months, dry skin, cold intolerance, and constipation. The patient was referred to the endocrinology clinic where physical examination revealed normal vital signs and delayed tendon reflex of the deep tendon reflex in the upper/lower extremities. The initial laboratory examination revealed hypopituitarism, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, polyuria, and hypertonic hypernatremia. The initial MRI scan showed a right-sided pituitary microadenoma. The patient was started on hydrocortisone and levothyroxine replacement therapy. Follow-up studies revealed an abnormal thickening of the infundibulum on the second MRI scan with no evidence of the microadenoma. New laboratory examination results confirmed the previous findings and ruled out the presence of autoimmune or inflammatory conditions. Tumor markers for germ cell tumors were negative. A water deprivation test confirmed central diabetes insipidus. Testosterone replacement and desmopressin (DDAVP) were added to the patient's therapy regimen. A tissue biopsy taken during transsphenoidal surgery revealed a positive result for an intrasellar pituitary germinoma confirmed by positive human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) staining, C-kit, and placental alkaline phosphatase (PLAP). A lumbar MRI scan and lumbar puncture were negative for metastatic disease. The patient was treated with whole ventricle brain radiation and showed subsequent clinical improvement. The patient was stable at the time of discharge.

Discharge Medications:
Hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, testosterone replacement, desmopressin (DDAVP)

Follow-up:
The patient is scheduled for follow-up visits with the endocrinology clinic to monitor treatment and evaluate persistent symptoms. Further imaging studies and laboratory tests may be ordered as indicated. Patients with intrasellar germinomas have a favorable prognosis and long-term follow-up is important to detect relapse or progression of residual disease.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 17-year-old female, was referred after 31 months of orthodontic treatment, with a history of surgical orthodontic traction resulting in an unfavorable outcome. The current anamneses and physical exam revealed an orthodontic device for space maintenance between teeth 12 and 14 and tooth 13 with clinical exposure of its crown on the palate and three orthodontic buttons present for elastic traction. Periapical and panoramic radiographic exams showed significant bone loss distal to 12 and mesial to 14, with tooth 13 apex constrained within the ennis inverted Y. 

After proper orthodontic treatment, the patient and parents were informed of the possible prosthetic rehabilitation alternatives and opted for partial maxillary osteotomy. The procedure, performed on March 02, 2001, comprised of the maxillary right canine removal and a partial maxillary osteotomy. 

Post-surgically, elastic traction was applied to conclude the approximation of the distal segment. Intermaxillary immobilization was sustained for 21 days, and during weekly postoperatory controls, the orthodontic arch-wire was substituted for a continuous arch to maintain stability of the segment and encourage the formation of a callus. 

Following the treatment, full orthodontic movements were cleared in April 24, 2001. Full treatment was concluded on October 23, 2001, and removable retainers were installed. The patient requested the removal of the internal rigid fixation on October 29, 2010. On the clinical and radiographic control of January 10 and 17, 2012, stability and pulpar vitality could be confirmed after 10 years and 10 months of follow-up with excellent periodontal conditions.

Patient Information:
Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 54
Sex: Female
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Admitting Diagnosis: Sodium hydroxide splash injury of left eye 
Final Diagnosis: Symblepharon with superficial and deep corneal neovascularization

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our eye emergency department with light perception in the left eye and congested eyelids and conjunctiva caused by a splash injury of sodium hydroxide. A diffuse corneal epithelial defect, stromal edema, and localized Descemet’s folds were observed during the initial examination. The patient was treated with 1% dexamethasone sodium phosphate drops, 1% atropine drops, and tobramycin. She was then given prednisone 50mg, daily for ten days, followed by a gradual taper by 5mg every 15 days. Despite frequent use of topical steroids, the patient developed a symblepharon and superficial and deep corneal neovascularization after three months.

Treatment:
A subconjunctival bevacizumab injection of 0.05ml (1.25mg) was administered to the left eye with the aim of reducing corneal neovascularization. The patient was advised to use 0.3% ofloxacin and 1% dexamethasone sodium phosphate drops three times daily for one week after the subconjunctival bevacizumab injection. A second subconjunctival bevacizumab injection was given when the vessels began to perfuse again two weeks after the first injection.

Outcome:
The patient's visual acuity improved to 0.1 logarithm of the minimum angle of resolution (LogMAR) two weeks after the second injection, and the corneal neovascularization was significantly reduced. During the next months, the patient's condition was well-controlled, and at the end of follow-up 24 months later, her VA and clinical condition were unaltered.

Admitting Diagnosis: Heart failure with renal artery aneurysm and arteriovenous fistula 

Principal Diagnosis at Discharge: Heart failure with renal artery aneurysm and arteriovenous fistula 

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted with complaints of dyspnea, lower extremity swelling, and abdominal distension. Physical examination revealed irregularly irregular rhythm, tender hepatomegaly, and bilateral lower extremity edema. Laboratory analysis showed elevated B-type Natriuretic Peptide (BNP) levels and transthoracic echocardiogram revealed right heart failure with dilated right atrium and ventricle.

Further evaluation with ultrasound and CT angiogram revealed a large renal artery aneurysm and arteriovenous fistula. The patient was deemed a poor surgical candidate and managed by endovascular occlusion. The aneurysm was completely obliterated using large coils and the feeding distal renal artery was occluded with Amplatzer vascular plug II.

Result:

Following endovascular occlusion, the patient's symptoms improved and the clinical exam showed resolution of jugular venous distention, decreased abdominal distension, and lower extremity edema. The ascites resolved on follow-up CT and BNP levels decreased at 6 months of follow-up.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient is advised to follow up with their primary care physician for further evaluation and management of heart failure and renal artery aneurysm. The patient should continue their medications and adhere to a low-salt diet. They are also advised to maintain a healthy lifestyle and avoid any activities that may cause undue stress or exertion.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: Vietnamese, 55-year-old male
Diagnosis: HBV cirrhosis without HDV, HCV or HIV coinfections
Complication: Grade 1 oesophageal varices

Hospital Course:
The patient was diagnosed with HBV cirrhosis without HDV, HCV or HIV coinfections in 1997. The probable route of infection was vertical transmission. After diagnosis, liver biopsy was done to confirm cirrhosis. The patient's condition was complicated by Grade 1 oesophageal varices and scored A5 in Child Pugh.

In August 1998, the patient started taking lamivudine at 100 mg/day due to the rising levels of HBV-DNA and ALT values. After 3 months of medication, the patient's HBV-DNA levels were undetectable by Digene assay. In February 1999, the patient's HBV-DNA levels were undetectable by qualitative PCR that had a sensitivity limit at 4 log10.

In January 2000, lamivudine medication was inadvertently stopped after only ten months of treatment. The patient was diagnosed with a relapse after the rising levels of HBV-DNA to 5.75 log10, ALT values at 3.1 ULN. The treatment continued for the next two years, where HBV-DNA was undetectable by quantitative PCR (cut-off at 2.3 log10, MONITOR COBAS, Roche), and ALT values were within the normal range.

In January 2002, HBV-DNA became detectable by PCR, and then, in June 2002, a viral breakthrough was documented with HBV-DNA levels at 9.2 log10 and ALT at 2.7 ULN. The patient was found to be asymptomatic. Upon sequencing of the HBV polymerase, two common lamivudine resistant mutations – rtL180M and rtM204V – were detected. To the ongoing lamivudine treatment, adefovir dipivoxil, 10 mg/day, was added; however, the following 10 months of treatment were uneventful, and HBV-DNA levels never fell below 5 log10. In June 2003, the HBV-DNA titer was 5.28 log10, and lamivudine medication was stopped, but adefovir was maintained; in addition, pegylated interferon α-2a was used as additional treatment. After five injections, the patient stopped pegylated interferon administration because of poor drug tolerance: anorexia, dry mouth, diarrhea, weight loss, and back pain. Thrombopenia was also detected.

After four months of uninterrupted adefovir monotherapy, HBV-DNA was still at 4.9 log10 and the same lamivudine resistant mutations were detected without adefovir resistant mutations. In September 2004, while on adefovir monotherapy, and 15 months after having stopped lamivudine and 13 months after having stopped pegylated interferon, HBV-DNA rose to 8.3 log10, ALT to 10 ULN and aspartate aminotransferase to 7 ULN. Prothrombin time was 78%, and total bilirubin and serum albumin were normal. Two adefovir resistant mutations, rtA181T and rtN236T, were detected.

The patient was then given a test trial of higher doses of adefovir (20 mg/day). However, after a month, HBV-DNA reached 7 log10 levels, ALT levels remained unchanged, and the patient's condition continued to deteriorate. The patient developed oedema, ascites, jaundice, mild renal insufficiency (serum creatinine 110 μmol/l), and a decreased prothrombin time (47% of normal). Therefore, tenofovir fumarate was started at a dose of 300 mg/day, while adefovir was continued for one month, and then it was stopped.

Two months later, HBV-DNA became undetectable by PCR, and the patient's prothrombin time level rose to 90%. The patient's jaundice and ascites also resolved. After eight months of tenofovir treatment, the patient's HBV-DNA was still undetectable by PCR on three separate occasions as of the most recent testing. 

Overall, the patient's condition remained unremarkable during the hospital stay. The patient is currently listed for liver transplantation as the treatment of HBV cirrhosis.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: Vietnamese, 55-year-old male
Diagnosis: HBV cirrhosis without HDV, HCV or HIV coinfections
Complication: Grade 1 oesophageal varices

Hospital Course:
The patient was diagnosed with HBV cirrhosis without HDV, HCV or HIV coinfections in 1997. The probable route of infection was vertical transmission. After diagnosis, liver biopsy was done to confirm cirrhosis. The patient's condition was complicated by Grade 1 oesophageal varices and scored A5 in Child Pugh.

In August 1998, the patient started taking lamivudine at 100 mg/day due to the rising levels of HBV-DNA and ALT values. After 3 months of medication, the patient's HBV-DNA levels were undetectable by Digene assay. In February 1999, the patient's HBV-DNA levels were undetectable by qualitative PCR that had a sensitivity limit at 4 log10.

In January 2000, lamivudine medication was inadvertently stopped after only ten months of treatment. The patient was diagnosed with a relapse after the rising levels of HBV-DNA to 5.75 log10, ALT values at 3.1 ULN. The treatment continued for the next two years, where HBV-DNA was undetectable by quantitative PCR (cut-off at 2.3 log10, MONITOR COBAS, Roche), and ALT values were within the normal range.

In January 2002, HBV-DNA became detectable by PCR, and then, in June 2002, a viral breakthrough was documented with HBV-DNA levels at 9.2 log10 and ALT at 2.7 ULN. The patient was found to be asymptomatic. Upon sequencing of the HBV polymerase, two common lamivudine resistant mutations – rtL180M and rtM204V – were detected. To the ongoing lamivudine treatment, adefovir dipivoxil, 10 mg/day, was added; however, the following 10 months of treatment were uneventful, and HBV-DNA levels never fell below 5 log10. In June 2003, the HBV-DNA titer was 5.28 log10, and lamivudine medication was stopped, but adefovir was maintained; in addition, pegylated interferon α-2a was used as additional treatment. After five injections, the patient stopped pegylated interferon administration because of poor drug tolerance: anorexia, dry mouth, diarrhea, weight loss, and back pain. Thrombopenia was also detected.

After four months of uninterrupted adefovir monotherapy, HBV-DNA was still at 4.9 log10 and the same lamivudine resistant mutations were detected without adefovir resistant mutations. In September 2004, while on adefovir monotherapy, and 15 months after having stopped lamivudine and 13 months after having stopped pegylated interferon, HBV-DNA rose to 8.3 log10, ALT to 10 ULN and aspartate aminotransferase to 7 ULN. Prothrombin time was 78%, and total bilirubin and serum albumin were normal. Two adefovir resistant mutations, rtA181T and rtN236T, were detected.

The patient was then given a test trial of higher doses of adefovir (20 mg/day). However, after a month, HBV-DNA reached 7 log10 levels, ALT levels remained unchanged, and the patient's condition continued to deteriorate. The patient developed oedema, ascites, jaundice, mild renal insufficiency (serum creatinine 110 μmol/l), and a decreased prothrombin time (47% of normal). Therefore, tenofovir fumarate was started at a dose of 300 mg/day, while adefovir was continued for one month, and then it was stopped.

Two months later, HBV-DNA became undetectable by PCR, and the patient's prothrombin time level rose to 90%. The patient's jaundice and ascites also resolved. After eight months of tenofovir treatment, the patient's HBV-DNA was still undetectable by PCR on three separate occasions as of the most recent testing. 

Overall, the patient's condition remained unremarkable during the hospital stay. The patient is currently listed for liver transplantation as the treatment of HBV cirrhosis.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [REDACTED]    Gender: Male    Date of Admission: [REDACTED]    Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

HOSPITAL COURSE:
2-day old male newborn was referred to us because of distended abdomen, abnormal genitalia and imperforate anus. Examination of genitalia revealed a well-formed double penis with normally located and functioning urethra, left penis had proximal hypospadias. There were normal penile shaft and bifid scrotum with each compartment containing a testicle. Perineal examination showed imperforate anus. The values of blood analysis were within normal ranges. Abdominal sonography showed distended bowel loops and bilateral normal kidneys. The patient underwent laparotomy and colostomy the day after admission, the colon was distended and duplicated.

Two months later, an intravenous pyelography was performed which showed normal kidneys and ureters. Voiding-cystourethrography revealed double bladder and urethra, but no vesicourethral reflux. At 4 months of age, surgical exploration of genitourinary tract showed the abnormal position of bladder and urethra. Cystoplasty and reimplantation of left ureter into a single bladder were performed. Left-side urethra with hypospadias was resected, and bifid scrotum repaired. Post-operative days passed without complication so that the patient could be discharged 2 weeks later.

At the age of one year, after colostogram and total colon evaluation, laparotomy, resection of duplicated recto-sigmoid colon and pull-through, and 3 months later colostomy closure was carried out. The patient was under observation until the age of 4 years when his parents decided to leave Iran due to family problems.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:
Abnormal Genitalia with Double Penis and Hypospadias, Imperforate Anus with Distended and Duplicated Bowel Loops, Duplicated Recto-Sigmoid Colon

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
Parents should schedule regular follow-up appointments with their primary care physician for monitoring and management of the patient's condition. They should also discuss any further diagnostic or treatment options with their healthcare provider if necessary. It is essential to follow a healthy diet and hygiene practices to prevent complications and discomfort.

Patient Name: [Name]
Sex: Female
Age: 40
Reason for Admission: Infertility Treatment

Hospital Course:

The patient was a 40-year-old woman who entered the hospital for infertility treatment and underwent a laparoscopic-assisted myomectomy. Timed intercourse was initiated three months after the surgery. The patient was diagnosed with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) based on an irregular cycle and high anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) levels. Standard treatment guidelines in Japan were followed, and the patient underwent timed intercourse with cyclofenil administered at a dose of 600 mg/d for 5 days, starting on cycle day 5 until cycle day 9. However, no follicular development was observed even on the 25th day of the menstrual cycle. The patient received 4 mg/d of chlormadinone acetate for 10 days, followed by timed intercourse with clomiphene citrate, which was administered at a dose of 50 mg/day for 5 days starting on cycle day 5 until cycle day 9. We observed a 48 × 41 mm anechoic mass in the patient's right ovary on the ultrasonogram on the 11th day of the menstrual cycle, which we initially considered a follicle and monitored its progress. Subsequent mass sizes on days 16th, 20th, 21st, and 28th mentioned the gradual change in the mass configuration. The mass disappeared on the 62nd day since detection (19th day of the menstrual cycle), and we diagnosed the mass as a HOC according to its clinical course.

Hospital Course Summary:

The 40-year-old female patient with a history of ureteral stones, Behcet's disease, and multiple myoma underwent a laparoscopic-assisted myomectomy for infertility treatment at our hospital. After the surgery, timed intercourse was initiated, and a diagnosis of PCOS was made based on an irregular cycle and high AMH levels. Treatment guidelines were followed, with the patient receiving medication to increase the chances of successful ovulation. A 48 × 41 mm anechoic mass was observed in the patient's right ovary, which was initially considered a follicle, but its course indicated it to be a HOC. The patient showed no symptoms, was closely monitored, and received follow-up without any medication for infertility treatment. The patient was discharged in good health, and further follow-up will be done during her next routine visit.

She is experiencing high anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) levels and underwent a laparoscopic-assisted myomectomy for myoma treatment.
